items.excerpt: A Cambridge University Press study found readers rated AI-generated stories higher than human-written ones — especially when they believed a human wrote them. The finding cuts at how publishers assess quality and how readers perceive authorship.

Tor Bramble is standing behind author HM Wolfe after The Atlantic reported that her dystopian romance Daggermouth scored 60% on the AI-detection tool Pangram. The case is becoming a test of whether detection scores can be trusted inside publishing workflows.
Writer and academic Jen Bowden argues LLMs still cannot capture regional dialect writing with any real success, making voice-rich fiction a differentiator in an era of generic AI prose.

If AI is helping researchers write, what happens to 'author voice' — long a core consideration for authors, editors and reviewers? Roohi Ghosh unpacks how AI-assisted drafting reshapes editorial judgement.

After a debut novel's six- and seven-figure deals were pulled over AI allegations, PW looks at what happens next for the author, the agents and the acquisition process that could not verify how the manuscript was made.

OpenAI has begun blocking prompts asking ChatGPT to write in the style of specific living authors. Style isn't explicitly protected by copyright, but the change reshapes what writers can ask an AI to do.
The EU AI Act's transparency rules now cover AI-generated or AI-manipulated content that could be mistaken for real — a labelling question publishers and authors selling into Europe have to answer.
Substack's site-wide AI detection rollout using Pangram has sparked confusion and false-positive fears among writers. Jane Friedman tracks what the scores actually mean for working authors.
Researchers at Stony Brook University say viral dark-romance bestseller Daggermouth contains roughly 60% AI-generated writing, putting detection tools at the centre of a bestseller controversy.
Books+Publishing's editorial surveys how thoroughly AI has seeped into every layer of the book trade — from manuscript authentication to scanning, licensing and bookseller supply.
Rare-books curator Kathryn James on why Anthropic found destructively scanning 'all the books in the world' easier than negotiating copyright — and what that does to the physical record.
AI allegations hit two seven-figure book deals in the same week — one publisher stood by its author, the other walked. ALLi reads what that split means for authors' AI-disclosure practices.
Dan Holloway covers the final approval of the Anthropic settlement, two new Simon & Schuster indie imprints and Canadian ebook pricing in this week's self-publishing news roundup.
